clinicalPearls: Failure to thrive describes inadequate physical growth in a young child, most often identified as weight gain that is poor for age or crosses downward through growth chart percentiles over time.
A single low measurement is less meaningful than the trajectory of serial measurements plotted on an appropriate growth chart.
The traditional split into organic and non-organic causes is artificial; many children have mixed contributors, and inadequate caloric intake is the final common pathway in most cases.
The three broad mechanisms are insufficient intake, inadequate absorption or increased losses, and increased energy requirements, and the history usually distinguishes among them.
A careful feeding, dietary, developmental, social, and psychosocial history plus observation of a feed often yields more than extensive laboratory testing.
Investigations should be guided by clues from the history and examination rather than performed as an indiscriminate panel.
Management prioritises adequate catch-up nutrition while addressing any medical, developmental, feeding, and psychosocial factors, often through a multidisciplinary approach.
Signs of neglect, abuse, or a threatening environment must be considered, but most children with faltering growth are not victims of maltreatment.
reference.pathophysiology: Growth requires that energy and nutrient intake exceed the demands of maintenance and activity. Faltering growth arises when this balance is disturbed: intake may be insufficient because of feeding difficulties, poor appetite, incorrect feed preparation, or limited food availability; nutrients may be inadequately absorbed or lost through malabsorption, chronic diarrhoea, or vomiting; or requirements may be raised by chronic illness such as cardiac, respiratory, renal, or inflammatory disease. Prolonged deficits deplete energy stores and, if sustained, can impair linear growth and, in severe or early cases, brain development. Psychosocial and caregiving factors frequently interact with these physiological mechanisms.
additionalDifferentials: Constitutional growth patterns and familial short stature (not true failure to thrive)
Chronic cardiac, respiratory, renal, or gastrointestinal disease
additionalInvestigations: Detailed dietary and feeding assessment with observation of a feed
Plotting of serial weight, length/height, and head circumference
Targeted first-line tests (full blood count, electrolytes, urinalysis) guided by findings
Coeliac serology and stool studies when malabsorption is suspected
Further specific testing directed by history and examination
redFlags: Severe or rapidly progressive weight loss or wasting
Signs of dehydration or micronutrient deficiency
Symptoms or signs pointing to serious underlying organic disease
reference.prognosis: With timely recognition and adequate nutritional rehabilitation most children achieve catch-up growth and do well, but prolonged or severe undernutrition, especially in infancy, can be associated with lasting effects on growth and neurodevelopment.
pitfalls: Diagnosing failure to thrive from a single measurement rather than the growth trend
Ordering broad laboratory panels instead of history-directed testing
Assuming an organic cause and overlooking feeding technique, caloric adequacy, or psychosocial factors
Mislabelling normal constitutional or genetically small children as failing to thrive
management: Nutritional rehabilitation with increased caloric and nutrient intake using energy-dense feeds and a structured feeding plan aimed at catch-up growth
Dietitian-led feeding support with correction of feed preparation and technique and treatment of feeding difficulties
Identification and treatment of any underlying organic cause such as coeliac disease, cow's milk protein allergy, gastro-oesophageal reflux or chronic illness
Addressing psychosocial and caregiving contributors with health-visitor and social support
Monitoring of serial weight, length or height and head circumference on growth charts, with vigilance for refeeding problems in severe undernutrition
Multidisciplinary involvement of paediatrics, dietetics, speech and language therapy for feeding, and social care
Safeguarding assessment where neglect is suspected, and admission or escalation for severe faltering growth or failed community management
